question: Unlike for other categories of student, most universities in Europe have yet to set specific enrolment fees for people with disabilities. Identifying individual challenges and characteristics student’s educational pathways is key to fostering equality of opportunity and building a society that values diversity, recognising the unique challenges that students with disabilities face in their academic career.

Article 14 and Article 26 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union enshrine, respectively, the right of all individuals to education and access to vocational and continuing training and the right of persons with disabilities to autonomous social and occupational integration.

Given that the objectives of the European strategy for universities adopted in 2022 include the fostering of diversity, inclusiveness and gender equality, can the Commission say whether EU legalisation is needed to introduce an enrolment fee for disabled students in all European universities, including a clear and comprehensive definition of the term 'disability' and taking into account the different physical and cognitive conditions of this category of students?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.7.2024) Under Article 165 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1, the EU shall contribute to the development of quality education by encouraging cooperation between Member States and, if necessary, by supporting and supplementing their action, while fully respecting the responsibility of the Member States for the organisation of their education systems.

Member States’ competence includes possible specific fees for people with disabilities. The provisions of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights are binding on the Member States when they are implementing EU law2.

The United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities to which the EU and all Member States are parties indicates that, signing members shall prohibit all discrimination based on disability and in relation to the right to education. They should also recognise the right of persons with disabilities to education.

On the basis of equal opportunity, states which are parties to the Convention shall ensure an inclusive education system at all levels and lifelong learning. In view of these commitments, the 2022 European strategy for universities3, which is a joint European vision for the higher education sector, seeks to foster diversity, inclusion and gender equality.

At EU level, the Erasmus+ programme4 is central to putting the policies into action by promoting equal opportunities and inclusion across its actions. Students with fewer opportunities can receive a monthly top-up grant in addition to their Erasmus+ individual support grant (criteria defined at national level). Participants can also be eligible for financial inclusion support based on real costs.
The latter is particularly relevant for students with disabilities.
